questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q1, key p.7.
questions.title: Most common cause of acute infective endocarditis in an IV drug user
questions.question: A 32-year-old IV drug user is admitted with high fever, chills and a rapidly progressive new regurgitant murmur. Which organism is most likely responsible for acute endocarditis in this setting?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Viridans streptococci cause the slower, subacute form of endocarditis on an already-damaged valve, not this fulminant, rapidly progressive picture.
explanations.B: Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of acute infective endocarditis, and in an intravenous drug user it classically seeds the tricuspid valve directly from injection-site bacteraemia. Its high virulence produces a fulminant illness within days -- high fever, rigors and rapid valve destruction with a new regurgitant murmur -- unlike the indolent course typical of lower-virulence organisms. This combination of an IV-drug-use risk factor with a rapidly evolving picture is the classic clinical fingerprint of acute S. aureus endocarditis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Staphylococcus epidermidis is a low-virulence skin commensal that causes indolent prosthetic-valve infection, not a fulminant acute presentation on a native valve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enterococcus faecalis is more typically associated with endocarditis following genitourinary or GI procedures in older patients, not this IV-drug-use acute presentation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Staphylococcus aureus as the most common cause of acute infective endocarditis, including in intravenous drug users.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q1, key p.7.
questions.title: Virulence factor letting Viridans streptococci adhere to a damaged valve
questions.question: Which virulence property explains why Viridans streptococci adhere to damaged valves?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Coagulase is a Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor that clots plasma; Viridans streptococci do not produce it.
explanations.B: Correct. Viridans streptococci synthesise dextran, a sticky extracellular polysaccharide, from dietary glucose. This dextran forms a biofilm that lets the organism adhere firmly to the fibrin-platelet vegetation already present on a damaged or abnormal heart valve, anchoring it in place against the flow of blood. This dextran-dependent adherence is exactly why Viridans streptococci need a pre-damaged valve to establish infection, rather than being able to seed a normal one the way S. aureus can.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus surface protein that binds immunoglobulin Fc regions; it plays no role in Viridans streptococcal adherence.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Novobiocin resistance is a laboratory identification feature of Staphylococcus saprophyticus, unrelated to valve adherence by Viridans streptococci.

questions.learning_objective: State that Viridans streptococci adhere to damaged heart valves via a dextran biofilm synthesised from glucose.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q1, key p.7.
questions.title: Best initial diagnostic test for suspected infective endocarditis
questions.question: A patient with suspected infective endocarditis -- best initial diagnostic specimen/test is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A throat swab samples the oropharynx, not the bloodstream, and cannot identify the organism infecting the heart valve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A single blood culture risks a false negative, and drawing it after antibiotics have already started can suppress bacterial growth and cause the culture to miss the causative organism.
explanations.C: Correct. Serial blood cultures -- at least three, from separate venepuncture sites, drawn before any antibiotic is given -- are the best initial investigation for suspected infective endocarditis. Because the bacteraemia of endocarditis is continuous, sampling on more than one occasion before treatment starts maximises the chance of isolating the organism and its susceptibilities. Starting empirical antibiotics first can sterilise the blood and permanently obscure the diagnosis, which is why cultures should be drawn first whenever the patient is stable enough to allow it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urine culture identifies a urinary pathogen, not the organism responsible for an infected heart valve.

questions.learning_objective: State that serial blood cultures drawn before antibiotics are the best initial investigation for suspected infective endocarditis.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q1, key p.7.
questions.title: Micro-embolic lesion on the palms/soles in acute endocarditis
questions.question: Which clinical sign is described as a micro-embolic lesion on the palms/soles in acute endocarditis?

explanations.A: Correct. Janeway lesions are small, painless, erythematous or haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles caused by septic micro-emboli that break off an infected valve and lodge in cutaneous small vessels. Because they are painless and flat, they are easy to overlook on examination, unlike the tender nodules of Osler nodes. Their presence in a febrile patient is a specific peripheral sign of infective endocarditis, especially the more embolising acute form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Osler nodes are painful, raised nodules on the finger and toe pads caused by immune-complex deposition, not painless embolic macules on the palms/soles.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with a pale centre, seen on fundoscopy, not a palm/sole skin finding.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Splinter haemorrhages are linear haemorrhages under the nail beds, a different peripheral sign from the palmar/plantar macules described here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Janeway lesions as painless, embolic macular lesions on the palms and soles in infective endocarditis.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q2, key p.7.
questions.title: Organism NOT covered by empiric endocarditis antimicrobial therapy
questions.question: Empiric antimicrobial coverage for suspected endocarditis should include activity against each of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS covered). MRSA is one of the leading bacterial causes of endocarditis, so empirical regimens include an agent active against it, such as vancomycin.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS covered). Viridans streptococci are the classic cause of subacute endocarditis, so empirical therapy is chosen to be active against them as well.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS covered). Enterococci are a recognised cause of endocarditis, particularly after genitourinary procedures, and empirical regimens are designed to cover them too.
explanations.D: Correct. Empirical antimicrobial therapy for suspected endocarditis is built to cover the bacteria that overwhelmingly cause the disease -- S. aureus/MRSA, Viridans streptococci and enterococci. Because endocarditis is essentially always a bacterial disease, this empirical cover has no antiviral activity, and Coxsackievirus B (a cause of a different disease, viral myocarditis) is not a target of it. Recognising this distinction keeps empirical treatment focused on the organisms that actually cause endocarditis rather than broadening it unnecessarily.

questions.learning_objective: State that empirical antimicrobial therapy for endocarditis targets bacterial pathogens (MRSA, Viridans streptococci, enterococci), not viruses.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q2, key p.7.
questions.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental extraction with a prosthetic valve
questions.question: A patient with a history of prosthetic valve placement is scheduled for dental extraction. What is the recommended prophylaxis:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A prosthetic valve is a recognised high-risk indication for endocarditis prophylaxis; omitting it would leave the patient unprotected during the procedure's bacteraemia.
explanations.B: Correct. A single dose of oral amoxicillin given shortly before a dental procedure is the recommended prophylaxis for a patient with a prosthetic valve. Dental extraction releases oral flora, chiefly Viridans streptococci, into the bloodstream, and amoxicillin covers this organism during the brief window of bacteraemia the procedure causes. This targeted, single-dose approach is reserved for patients whose valve is already abnormal or artificial, since it is the damaged or prosthetic surface that lets a transient bacteraemia progress to endocarditis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Monthly benzathine penicillin is the secondary-prophylaxis regimen used to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever, not single-procedure endocarditis prophylaxis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Erythromycin before a procedure is not the standard first-line dental prophylaxis; it is used as an alternative in patients with a penicillin allergy.

questions.learning_objective: State that a single dose of oral amoxicillin before a dental procedure is standard endocarditis prophylaxis for an at-risk patient.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q2, key p.7.
questions.title: Pathogenesis of prosthetic-valve endocarditis due to S. epidermidis
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of prosthetic-valve endocarditis due to S. epidermidis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. S. epidermidis does not produce a potent myocardial-necrosing toxin; its pathogenesis is a device-surface colonisation process, not toxin-mediated tissue destruction.
explanations.B: Correct. Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative skin commensal, colonises a prosthetic valve by forming a glycocalyx (slime) biofilm on the artificial surface. This biofilm cements the organism and subsequent generations to the device, shielding it from both host immune defences and antibiotics. Because this is a surface-biofilm process rather than tissue invasion, S. epidermidis prosthetic-valve infection is often indolent and difficult to eradicate with antibiotics alone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Molecular mimicry with valve antigens describes the immune-mediated mechanism of rheumatic fever, not S. epidermidis prosthetic-valve infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. S. epidermidis reaches a prosthetic valve via bacteraemia introduced at the time of surgery or device handling, not by direct spread from an adjacent lung infection.

questions.learning_objective: State that Staphylococcus epidermidis colonises prosthetic valves chiefly by glycocalyx (biofilm) formation on the device surface.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q2, key p.7.
questions.title: Most common viral cause of myocarditis
questions.question: A 24-year-old presents with dyspnea and signs of heart failure after a recent viral illness. Which organism is listed as the most common viral cause of myocarditis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Influenza virus can rarely cause myocarditis, but it is not the most common viral cause.
explanations.B: Correct. Coxsackievirus B, an enterovirus, is the most common viral cause of myocarditis, owing to its specific tropism for cardiac myocytes. After an initial viraemia the virus infects the myocardium directly, producing cell injury through both direct viral cytolysis and the accompanying immune response. A previously well young person who develops dyspnoea and heart failure after a preceding viral-type illness should raise suspicion for Coxsackievirus B myocarditis specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cytomegalovirus can cause myocarditis, particularly in immunocompromised hosts, but it is not the most common cause overall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Epstein-Barr virus is a rarer cause of myocarditis, well behind Coxsackievirus B in frequency.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Coxsackievirus B as the most common viral cause of myocarditis.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q2, key p.7.
questions.title: Diagnostic features emphasized for myocarditis
questions.question: Which diagnostic features are emphasized for myocarditis?

options.A: Elevated cardiac enzymes and heart-failure presentation
options.B: Positive blood cultures and new murmur

explanations.A: Correct. Myocarditis is diagnosed from a combination of elevated cardiac enzymes (such as troponin), which rise as inflamed myocytes are injured, together with a clinical presentation of heart failure -- dyspnoea, fatigue and reduced cardiac output. This combination, rather than a murmur or a positive blood culture, is the pattern that should point the clinician toward myocarditis as the underlying diagnosis. Direct viral injury and the accompanying immune response damage myocytes enough both to release troponin and to impair contractile function.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Positive blood cultures and a new murmur are the hallmark findings of infective endocarditis, a valve infection, not myocarditis, which is inflammation of the heart muscle itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Optochin sensitivity is a laboratory test used to identify Streptococcus pneumoniae on culture, unrelated to the clinical diagnosis of myocarditis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myocarditis is not diagnosed from skin findings; those belong to other conditions such as endocarditis (Janeway lesions) or rheumatic fever.

questions.learning_objective: State that myocarditis is diagnosed from elevated cardiac enzymes together with a heart-failure presentation.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q2, key p.7.
questions.title: Causative organism of cardiac manifestations weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis
questions.question: A patient presents with cardiac manifestations developing 2-4 weeks after an episode of streptococcal pharyngitis. Laboratory investigation focuses on a pathogen whose virulence factor triggers an immune-mediated cross-reaction with cardiac tissue. Serologic testing is used to demonstrate a recent infection. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus causes acute infective endocarditis directly, not a delayed immune-mediated cardiac disease following pharyngitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Viridans streptococci cause subacute endocarditis by direct valve colonisation, not a delayed immune-mediated syndrome after pharyngitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Staphylococcus epidermidis causes indolent prosthetic-device infection, unrelated to a preceding streptococcal throat infection.
explanations.D: Correct. Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus) is the organism responsible: acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis when antibodies raised against the organism's M protein cross-react with joint, heart and brain antigens, producing cardiac and other manifestations some 2-4 weeks later. Because the heart is not directly infected at this stage, serologic testing (such as the antistreptolysin O titer) rather than a positive culture is used to demonstrate the antecedent streptococcal infection. This delayed, immune cross-reactive pattern -- not direct bacterial invasion -- is the hallmark that identifies S. pyogenes as the trigger organism.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Streptococcus pyogenes as the causative organism whose antecedent pharyngitis triggers acute rheumatic fever.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q3, key p.7.
questions.title: Diagnosis suggested by chest pain worsening with inspiration/coughing after pneumonia
questions.question: A patient develops chest pain that worsens with inspiration and coughing and has a recent pneumonia. The lecture indicates the most likely diagnosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Myocarditis typically presents with heart-failure symptoms and elevated cardiac enzymes, not pleuritic, positional chest pain.
explanations.B: Correct. Pericarditis classically presents with sharp, pleuritic chest pain that worsens with inspiration and coughing, reflecting irritation of the pain-sensitive parietal pericardium; the pain is often eased by sitting forward. A recent pneumonia is a recognised route by which infection spreads directly to the pericardium from an adjacent focus in the lung. This combination -- pleuritic, positional chest pain following a respiratory infection -- is the clinical pattern that points to pericarditis rather than a coronary or myocardial event.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Endocarditis presents with fever, a new murmur and embolic phenomena, not pleuritic chest pain tied to breathing and coughing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pulmonary embolism can cause pleuritic chest pain but does not explain the specific link to a preceding pneumonia emphasised here, which points instead to direct spread to the pericardium.

questions.learning_objective: State that acute pericarditis classically presents with chest pain that worsens with inspiration and coughing.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q3, key p.7.
questions.title: Common cause(s) of purulent (infective) pericarditis
questions.question: Which pathogen(s) is/are common cause(s) of purulent (infective) pericarditis?

explanations.A: Correct. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a recognised cause of purulent (suppurative) pericarditis, typically reaching the pericardium either by direct extension from an adjacent pneumonic focus in the lung or by haematogenous seeding during pneumococcal bacteraemia. Purulent pericarditis is a medical emergency because of the risk of cardiac tamponade and later constriction, so identifying a recognised bacterial cause such as S. pneumoniae guides both antibiotic choice and the urgency of drainage. This is a distinct, more aggressive process than the milder, self-limiting viral pericarditis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Coxsackievirus and echovirus cause viral pericarditis, which is typically self-limiting and serous, not purulent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Viridans streptococci are the classic cause of subacute infective endocarditis on a damaged valve, not a typical cause of purulent pericarditis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an atypical respiratory pathogen, not a typical cause of purulent pericarditis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Streptococcus pneumoniae as a recognised cause of purulent (infective) pericarditis.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q3, key p.7.
questions.title: Enterovirus most likely isolated from stool in a teenager with acute myocarditis
questions.question: A 16-year-old male developed chest pain and dyspnea, which gradually worsened. He was examined in the Emergency Department where tachycardia and signs of heart failure were noted. Electrocardiographic changes were seen and chest x-ray revealed cardiomegaly. An enterovirus was isolated from a stool specimen. Which of the following was the agent most likely isolated?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Enterovirus 70 is classically associated with acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis, not myocarditis.
explanations.B: Correct. When an enterovirus is isolated from stool in a patient presenting with acute myocarditis (tachycardia, heart failure, ECG changes and cardiomegaly), Coxsackievirus B is the most likely agent recovered. Coxsackievirus B enters by the faecal-oral route, replicates first in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, and is shed in stool during this phase, before a secondary viraemia seeds the myocardium because of the virus's cardiac tropism. This two-stage pattern -- detectable in stool, then producing cardiac disease -- is the classic picture for Coxsackievirus B myocarditis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is a bacterium, not an enterovirus, and would not be recovered by stool virus isolation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coxsackievirus A causes a more focal myositis pattern and is less strongly linked to myocarditis than Coxsackievirus B.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Viridans streptococci are bacteria that cause endocarditis, not an enterovirus recoverable from stool.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Coxsackievirus B as the enterovirus most likely isolated from stool in a patient with acute myocarditis.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q4, key p.7.
questions.title: Mechanism underlying cardiac manifestations after streptococcal pharyngitis with migratory polyarthritis
questions.question: A 9-year-old boy develops migratory polyarthritis and fever two weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis. The mechanism underlying the cardiac manifestations of his illness is best described as:

options.A: Direct bacterial invasion of heart valves

explanations.A: Incorrect. There is no direct bacterial invasion of the heart in rheumatic fever; the streptococcal infection is confined to the throat, and the cardiac disease follows afterward through an immune mechanism.
explanations.B: Correct. Acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis when antibodies raised against the group A streptococcal M protein cross-react with antigens in the heart, joints and brain -- molecular mimicry, classically described as a type II hypersensitivity mechanism. This cross-reactivity, rather than ongoing bacterial invasion, is what produces the carditis, migratory polyarthritis and other manifestations that appear roughly two to four weeks after the original throat infection. Recognising this mechanism also explains why penicillin given at this stage cannot reverse the cardiac damage that has already resulted from the immune cross-reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rheumatic fever's cardiac injury is attributed to direct antibody cross-reactivity with tissue antigens, not primarily to circulating immune-complex deposition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Group A Streptococcus does not act through an endotoxin (a Gram-negative cell-wall component); the mechanism here is antibody cross-reactivity, not septic/endotoxic damage.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cardiac manifestations of rheumatic fever result from immune cross-reactivity (molecular mimicry) rather than direct bacterial invasion.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q4, key p.7.
questions.title: Specific laboratory test for past streptococcal infection in suspected rheumatic fever
questions.question: Which laboratory test is a specific test for diagnosing past streptococcal infection in suspected rheumatic fever?

options.C: Blood culture positive for S. pyogenes

explanations.A: Correct. The antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer measures antibodies against streptolysin O, a toxin secreted by group A Streptococcus, and is a specific serologic marker of a recent or past streptococcal infection. Because rheumatic fever is immune-mediated and appears weeks after the original pharyngitis, direct throat or blood culture is often already negative by the time cardiac or joint symptoms develop; a titer above roughly 200 IU/mL instead documents that a streptococcal infection occurred in the preceding weeks. Together with the Jones criteria, this raised ASO titer is one of the required pieces of laboratory evidence needed to secure the diagnosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By the time rheumatic fever manifests, the original throat infection has usually resolved, so a throat culture is frequently negative and does not reliably document the antecedent infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rheumatic fever is not caused by ongoing bacteraemia, so a blood culture would not be expected to grow S. pyogenes at this stage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A negative Anti-DNAse B result would argue against, not support, evidence of a recent streptococcal infection; a raised, not negative, titer is what is diagnostically useful.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer as a specific serologic marker of past streptococcal infection supporting a rheumatic fever diagnosis.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q4, key p.7.
questions.title: Best statement describing rheumatic fever after streptococcal pharyngitis and new mitral murmur
questions.question: A 12-year-old girl experiences a group A streptococcus pharyngitis and within 3 weeks has chest pain and develops new murmurs of mitral regurgitation. Which of the following statements best typed the disease she is suffering?

options.A: It is a complication of group A streptococcal skin disease but usually not of pharyngitis.
options.B: It is characterized by inflammatory lesions that may involve the heart, joints, subcutaneous tissues, and CNS.
options.C: Prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin is of little value.
options.D: The pathogenesis is due to type III hypersensitivity reaction.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rheumatic fever is classically a complication of streptococcal pharyngitis, not skin infection -- the reverse of what this option states.
explanations.B: Correct. Acute rheumatic fever is a multisystem inflammatory disease: it can involve the heart (carditis, seen here as new mitral regurgitation), the joints (migratory polyarthritis), subcutaneous tissue (subcutaneous nodules) and the central nervous system (Sydenham's chorea). This girl's presentation, chest pain and a new regurgitant murmur three weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis, fits this classic multisystem pattern that defines the disease. Recognising rheumatic fever as multisystem, rather than a disease confined to the heart alone, is central to applying the Jones diagnostic criteria correctly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Benzathine penicillin secondary prophylaxis is of substantial, well-established value in preventing recurrent attacks and further cardiac damage, not of little value.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pathogenesis of rheumatic fever is most commonly described as type II hypersensitivity (antibody cross-reactivity with tissue antigens via molecular mimicry), not type III (immune-complex-mediated).

questions.learning_objective: State that acute rheumatic fever is a multisystem disease that can involve the heart, joints, subcutaneous tissue and CNS.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q4, key p.7.
questions.title: Lab clue distinguishing Viridans streptococci from S. pneumoniae in subacute endocarditis
questions.question: A 28-year-old with suspected subacute bacterial endocarditis: which agar/biochemical clue helps distinguish Viridans streptococci from S. pneumoniae?

options.A: Viridans is optochin resistant and bile insoluble
options.B: Viridans is optochin sensitive and bile soluble

explanations.A: Correct. Both Viridans streptococci and Streptococcus pneumoniae are alpha-haemolytic on blood agar and can look identical on culture and Gram stain, but two simple tests separate them: Viridans streptococci are resistant to optochin and insoluble in bile, whereas S. pneumoniae is optochin-sensitive and lyses (is soluble) in the presence of bile salts because of its autolytic enzyme system. This distinction matters clinically because Viridans streptococci are the classic cause of subacute endocarditis, while S. pneumoniae is not, so confirming optochin resistance and bile insolubility supports the suspected diagnosis here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes S. pneumoniae's own reactions (optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble), the reverse of the Viridans streptococcal pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Both organisms are catalase-negative streptococci; catalase positivity is a staphylococcal feature, not a way to distinguish these two streptococci.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Novobiocin resistance is the test used to identify Staphylococcus saprophyticus among coagulase-negative staphylococci, unrelated to differentiating these two streptococci.

questions.learning_objective: State that Viridans streptococci are distinguished from Streptococcus pneumoniae by optochin resistance and bile insolubility.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q4, key p.7.
questions.title: Pattern of staphylococcal sepsis progressing to valve destruction with distant emboli
questions.question: A hospitalized patient with staphylococcal sepsis later develops acute valve destruction with embolic phenomena to the brain and spleen. This pattern is most consistent with:

options.A: Subacute endocarditis due to Viridans streptococci
options.B: Acute endocarditis due to Staphylococcus aureus
options.C: Viral myocarditis due to Coxsackie virus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Subacute Viridans endocarditis follows a slow, indolent course with low-grade fever, not rapid valve destruction with septic emboli to the brain and spleen.
explanations.B: Correct. Rapid valve destruction with septic emboli to distant organs such as the brain and spleen, developing after documented staphylococcal sepsis, is the characteristic pattern of acute Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis. S. aureus's toxins and enzymes destroy valve leaflets quickly, and the resulting vegetations fragment easily, throwing septic emboli into the systemic circulation within days. Recognising this rapidly destructive, embolic pattern after staphylococcal bacteraemia should prompt urgent echocardiography and consideration of early surgical intervention.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Viral myocarditis inflames the heart muscle itself and does not produce valve destruction or septic emboli, which require an infected valve as the embolic source.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rheumatic fever carditis is an immune-mediated inflammatory process, not an embolic, valve-destroying infection following staphylococcal sepsis.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise acute valve destruction with septic emboli to the brain and spleen after staphylococcal sepsis as the pattern of acute S. aureus endocarditis.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q5, key p.7.
questions.title: Correct management statement for myocarditis
questions.question: In myocarditis, which of the following management statements is correct?

options.A: There is a specific universally effective antimicrobial for viral myocarditis
options.B: Most causes have no specific cure; supportive care is often given

explanations.A: Incorrect. There is no antiviral agent with proven universal efficacy against the common viral causes of myocarditis, including Coxsackievirus B.
explanations.B: Correct. For the great majority of causes of myocarditis, particularly viral myocarditis, there is no specific antimicrobial cure. Management is therefore supportive: treating heart failure, arrhythmias and haemodynamic complications as they arise while the patient's own immune response clears the underlying infection, sometimes with mechanical circulatory support in severe cases. Recognising that there is no curative antimicrobial for most myocarditis keeps management focused on early recognition and supportive treatment of complications.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Myocarditis affects the heart muscle, not the valves, so valve replacement plays no role in its management.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Erythromycin is an antibacterial with no activity against the viruses that cause most myocarditis, and lifelong use is not a recognised preventive measure for it.

questions.learning_objective: State that most causes of myocarditis have no specific cure and are managed supportively.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q5, key p.7.
questions.title: Organism identified by GPC clusters, catalase+/coagulase+ causing acute endocarditis with tricuspid murmur
questions.question: A 34-year-old man was in his usual state of health until last night, when he felt feverish, had a shaking chill, and became short of breath at rest. Temperature 39C, blood pressure 110/60, pulse 104, respirations 18. Scattered rakes were heard in both bases. A new murmur consistent with tricuspid insufficiency was heard. Gram-positive cocci in clusters grew in blood culture. It is catalase positive and coagulase positive. Which of the following organisms is the most likely etiologic agent of his acute endocarditis case?

explanations.A: Correct. Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are both catalase-positive and coagulase-positive identify Staphylococcus aureus, the leading cause of acute infective endocarditis. The acute onset with high fever, rigors and a new tricuspid regurgitant murmur fits the fulminant, right-sided pattern typical of S. aureus endocarditis. Coagulase positivity is the key laboratory feature that separates S. aureus from the coagulase-negative staphylococci (such as S. epidermidis), which cause a much more indolent disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase-negative, which does not match this patient's coagulase-positive culture result.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is also coagulase-negative, and it is primarily a urinary pathogen, not a typical cause of acute endocarditis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a catalase-negative diplococcus, not a catalase-positive, coagulase-positive cluster-forming coccus.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Streptococcus pyogenes is also catalase-negative and grows in chains, not clusters, and it does not typically cause acute infective endocarditis directly.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Staphylococcus aureus (catalase-positive, coagulase-positive GPC clusters) as the cause of acute endocarditis in this vignette.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q5, key p.7.
questions.title: Finding NOT part of the Jones major criteria for rheumatic fever
questions.question: Which of the following is not part of the classical Jones major criteria for rheumatic fever?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a major criterion). Migratory polyarthritis, arthritis moving from joint to joint, is one of the classical Jones major criteria.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a major criterion). Rheumatic carditis, inflammation of the heart valves and myocardium, is one of the classical Jones major criteria.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a major criterion). Sydenham's chorea, involuntary movements from CNS involvement, is one of the classical Jones major criteria.
explanations.D: Correct. Painless macular haemorrhages on the palms describe Janeway lesions, a peripheral sign of infective endocarditis, not a feature of rheumatic fever. Acute rheumatic fever's own features -- carditis, migratory polyarthritis, chorea, subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum -- are a distinct set from the embolic skin signs of endocarditis. Recognising this distractor is a common way exam questions test whether a student can tell the two related but separate cardiovascular-infection syndromes apart.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the features of rheumatic fever from Janeway lesions, a finding of infective endocarditis rather than rheumatic fever.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q6, key p.7.
questions.title: Role of penicillin given after onset of rheumatic fever with established carditis
questions.question: A patient with rheumatic carditis arrives late after onset of RF. According to your study, what is the role of giving penicillin after RF onset?

options.B: No benefit from penicillin after onset of rheumatic fever
options.C: Penicillin is contraindicated after RF onset

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rheumatic carditis is immune-mediated tissue injury that has already occurred by the time symptoms appear; killing any residual bacteria cannot reverse damage that is not itself an ongoing infection.
explanations.B: Correct. Penicillin given once rheumatic fever has already begun eradicates any remaining group A streptococcal infection, but it does not reverse carditis that has already been established by the immune-mediated inflammatory process. Because rheumatic fever is driven by cross-reactive antibodies rather than ongoing bacterial invasion of the heart, there is no benefit to the carditis itself from penicillin given at this late stage. Penicillin remains essential nonetheless -- to clear any lingering infection and as the basis of long-term secondary prophylaxis against future attacks -- but it will not undo carditis that has already developed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Penicillin is not contraindicated after RF onset; it is still indicated to clear any residual infection and to begin secondary prophylaxis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Penicillin has no direct effect on chorea, which is a CNS manifestation that resolves gradually on its own over weeks to months, not within 24 hours of any treatment.

questions.learning_objective: State that penicillin given after the onset of rheumatic fever does not reverse established rheumatic carditis.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q1, key p.9.
questions.title: Effect of Coxsackie B virus in suckling mice
questions.question: Which of the following is a result of Coxsackie B virus in a suckling mice?

options.B: Wide spread myositis and flaccid paralysis

explanations.A: Correct. In the classic suckling-mouse laboratory model historically used to characterise the Coxsackieviruses, Coxsackievirus B produces widespread (generalised) myositis together with encephalitis and other visceral involvement, reflecting the virus's broad tissue tropism. This experimental multi-organ pattern mirrors Coxsackievirus B's clinical tropism for the heart, meninges and pancreas in humans, which is part of why it is recognised as cardiotropic. The distinct pattern each Coxsackievirus group produces in this model is what historically let virologists tell group A and group B apart before modern typing methods existed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Widespread myositis with flaccid paralysis is the pattern classically produced by Coxsackievirus A in this model, not Coxsackievirus B.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Only the focal myositis-and-encephalitis pattern (option A) is the classic Coxsackievirus B result; the flaccid-paralysis pattern belongs to group A, so both cannot be correct together as stated.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coxsackievirus B does produce a recognised, well-described pattern in suckling mice (myositis with encephalitis), so 'none of the above' is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that Coxsackievirus B produces myositis together with encephalitis in the suckling-mouse laboratory model.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q2, key p.9.
questions.title: Route that is NOT a typical mode of transmission for pericarditis pathogens
questions.question: Which of the following is not a typical mode of transmission for pericarditis pathogens?

options.B: Direct spread from adjacent thoracic structures

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS typical). Bacteraemia or viraemia commonly seeds the pericardium via the bloodstream, a recognised route of pericardial infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS typical). Direct extension from an adjacent infected structure, such as the lung or pleura, is a well-recognised route to the pericardium -- explaining pericarditis after pneumonia.
explanations.C: Correct. Pathogens reach the pericardium chiefly by haematogenous spread, direct extension from an adjacent thoracic structure, or spread from an already-infected myocardium. There is no direct airway-to-pericardium route, so simply inhaling contaminated air is not itself a way that pathogens reach the pericardial space, in contrast to the way inhalation can seed the lungs directly. Recognising this helps explain why pericarditis follows a pneumonia or a systemic bacteraemic illness rather than direct exposure to airborne organisms.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS typical). Infection can spread directly from an already-infected myocardium to the adjacent pericardium, a recognised route of pericardial infection.

questions.learning_objective: State that pericarditis pathogens spread by haematogenous, direct or myocardial routes, not by inhalation of contaminated air.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q2, key p.9.
questions.title: Diagnosis suggested by migratory polyarthritis, fever and recent pharyngitis with raised ASO
questions.question: A 10-year-old child presents with migratory polyarthritis, fever, and a recent history of pharyngitis. ASO titer is elevated. Which condition is most likely?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute endocarditis presents with fever, a new murmur and embolic phenomena, not migratory polyarthritis, and it is not typically linked to a raised ASO titer.
explanations.B: Correct. Acute rheumatic fever presents with fever and migratory polyarthritis (one of its major clinical features), developing after an antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis, with an elevated ASO titer providing serologic confirmation of that antecedent infection. This combination of a preceding sore throat, migratory joint involvement, fever and a raised ASO titer is the classic diagnostic pattern for rheumatic fever, distinct from the direct-infection syndromes of endocarditis, myocarditis or pericarditis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Myocarditis presents with heart-failure symptoms and elevated cardiac enzymes, not migratory polyarthritis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pericarditis presents with pleuritic chest pain, not migratory polyarthritis, and is not the classic condition linked to a raised ASO titer after pharyngitis.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise migratory polyarthritis, fever after pharyngitis and a raised ASO titer as the diagnostic pattern of rheumatic fever.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q3, key p.9.
questions.title: Mode of transmission of Coxsackie virus
questions.question: How is the mode of transmission of Coxsackie virus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inhalation is the route for many respiratory viruses, but it is not the primary transmission route for Coxsackievirus.
explanations.B: Correct. Like other enteroviruses, Coxsackievirus is transmitted primarily by the faecal-oral route -- ingestion of virus shed in the stool of an infected person, typically via contaminated hands, food or water. The virus is acid-stable and survives passage through the stomach, establishing an initial infection in the gastrointestinal tract before any subsequent viraemia and spread to target organs such as the heart. This transmission route explains why Coxsackievirus infections cluster in settings of poor sanitation or close contact among young children.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Simple skin contact is not the recognised primary transmission route for Coxsackievirus; ingestion is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Direct skin penetration is not how Coxsackievirus is transmitted; it is acquired by ingestion via the faecal-oral route.

questions.learning_objective: State that Coxsackievirus is transmitted by the faecal-oral route.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q3, key p.9.
questions.title: Primary site of multiplication for Coxsackie viruses
questions.question: The primary site of multiplication for Coxsackie viruses is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The liver is not the primary replication site for Coxsackievirus; it replicates first in the gut before any systemic spread.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Heart muscle is a target organ Coxsackievirus reaches only after a secondary viraemia, not its primary site of replication.
explanations.C: Correct. After ingestion, Coxsackievirus replicates primarily in the lymphoid tissue of the gastrointestinal tract (Peyer's patches and associated mucosal lymphoid tissue) before a secondary viraemia disseminates it to distant, cardiotropic and neurotropic target organs. This two-stage pattern -- local GI replication followed by systemic spread -- explains both why the virus is detectable in stool early in infection and why clinical disease such as myocarditis can appear some days after the initial gastrointestinal phase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The central nervous system is a target organ reached secondarily via viraemia, not the primary site of Coxsackievirus multiplication.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primary site of Coxsackievirus multiplication is the lymphoid tissue of the gastrointestinal tract.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q4, key p.9.
questions.title: Diseases caused by Coxsackie B virus
questions.question: Which of the following are diseases caused by Coxsackie B virus?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS correct, but not the complete answer). Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease) is a genuine Coxsackievirus B disease, but it is not the only one listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS correct, but not the complete answer). Myocarditis is a genuine Coxsackievirus B disease, but it is not the only one listed.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS correct, but not the complete answer). Coxsackievirus B has been implicated as an environmental trigger for type 1 diabetes mellitus, but this is not the only disease listed.
explanations.D: Correct. Coxsackievirus B's broad tissue tropism -- muscle, heart, pancreas and pleura -- explains why a single virus produces this spread of clinical associations: direct myositis producing pleurodynia (Bornholm disease, epidemic myalgia with pleuritic chest pain), cardiotropic infection producing myocarditis, and beta-cell injury or immune triggering implicated as an environmental factor in type 1 diabetes mellitus. Recognising this spectrum helps explain why a single Coxsackievirus B infection can be raised in the differential for such different clinical presentations.

questions.learning_objective: State that Coxsackievirus B is associated with pleurodynia, myocarditis and a role in type 1 diabetes mellitus.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q4, key p.9.
questions.title: Organism that is NOT a common causative agent of pericarditis
questions.question: Which of the following is not a common causative agent of pericarditis?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a common cause). Staphylococcus aureus commonly causes purulent pericarditis by haematogenous spread.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a common cause). Streptococcus pneumoniae commonly causes purulent pericarditis, often by direct spread from pneumonia.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a common cause). Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a leading cause of pericarditis, especially where tuberculosis is endemic.
explanations.D: Correct. Among the recognised bacterial causes of pericarditis -- Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis -- Streptococcus pyogenes is not a typical direct cause, even though it is the trigger organism for the separate, immune-mediated condition of rheumatic pericarditis. S. aureus, S. pneumoniae and M. tuberculosis all directly infect the pericardium by haematogenous spread or direct extension, whereas S. pyogenes more often causes cardiac inflammation indirectly, through the immune cross-reactivity of rheumatic fever, rather than by directly infecting the pericardium.

questions.learning_objective: State that Streptococcus pyogenes is not a typical direct causative organism of infective pericarditis.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q5, key p.9.
questions.title: Feature that is NOT typical of subacute infective endocarditis
questions.question: Which of the following is not a typical clinical feature of subacute endocarditis?

explanations.A: Correct. Subacute infective endocarditis, classically caused by Viridans streptococci on an already-damaged valve, presents with a low-grade, indolent fever, not the high spiking fever with rigors seen in acute disease. Because subacute endocarditis develops gradually from a lower-virulence organism establishing itself on an already-abnormal valve, the resulting inflammatory and febrile response is correspondingly mild rather than the intense, spiking pattern produced by a highly virulent organism such as S. aureus in acute endocarditis. High spiking fever with rigors is instead a feature of the fulminant, acute form of the disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS typical). Low-grade, indolent fever is a classic feature of subacute endocarditis.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS typical). Splinter haemorrhages are a classic peripheral finding of subacute endocarditis.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS typical). Night sweats are a classic constitutional symptom of subacute endocarditis.

questions.learning_objective: State that high spiking fever with rigors is not typical of subacute infective endocarditis, which instead presents with a low-grade fever.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q5, key p.9.
questions.title: Family under which Coxsackie viruses are classified
questions.question: Coxsackie viruses are classified under which family?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Herpesviridae are large, enveloped DNA viruses, structurally unrelated to the small, non-enveloped RNA Coxsackievirus.
explanations.B: Correct. Coxsackievirus is an enterovirus within the family Picornaviridae, a family of small, non-enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses that also includes poliovirus, echovirus, rhinovirus and hepatitis A virus. Its lack of an envelope makes it resistant to gastric acid and bile, well-suited to faecal-oral transmission and gut replication, and its positive-sense RNA genome can be translated directly by host ribosomes. Recognising this family membership groups Coxsackievirus, for teaching purposes, with these other non-enveloped RNA viruses despite their very different clinical diseases.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flaviviridae are enveloped RNA viruses (such as dengue and yellow fever virus), a different family from the non-enveloped Coxsackievirus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Retroviridae are enveloped RNA viruses that replicate via a DNA intermediate (such as HIV), structurally and replicatively unrelated to Coxsackievirus.

questions.learning_objective: State that Coxsackievirus is classified within the family Picornaviridae.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q5, key p.9.
questions.title: Non-specific test(s) for the diagnosis of rheumatic fever
questions.question: Which test is non-specific for the diagnosis of rheumatic fever?

explanations.A: Incorrect. ASO is the specific serologic marker of past streptococcal infection in rheumatic fever, the opposite of non-specific.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this alone is not the complete answer). ESR is indeed non-specific, but CRP is equally non-specific and should be included too.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this alone is not the complete answer). CRP is indeed non-specific, but ESR is equally non-specific and should be included too.
explanations.D: Correct. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are both non-specific acute-phase reactants that rise with any systemic inflammation, infectious or non-infectious. In the diagnostic work-up for rheumatic fever they serve only as supportive minor criteria of ongoing inflammation, unlike the antistreptolysin O titer, which specifically documents antecedent streptococcal infection. A raised ESR or CRP therefore adds supportive evidence of active inflammation, but neither can on its own confirm the diagnosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that ESR and CRP are non-specific acute-phase markers used as supportive, not diagnostic, evidence in rheumatic fever.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q6, key p.9.
questions.title: Complication of Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection
questions.question: Which of the following is a complication of Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection?

explanations.A: Correct. Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces an exotoxin that, once absorbed systemically from the local throat infection, can damage the myocardium, producing toxin-mediated myocarditis as a serious complication of diphtheria. The toxin inhibits protein synthesis in susceptible cells, and the myocardium is particularly vulnerable, producing myocyte injury with conduction abnormalities and heart failure. Myocarditis is one of the most feared complications of diphtheria because it can cause sudden cardiac death even after the local throat infection has been treated, which is why diphtheria antitoxin is given early.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Endocarditis is not a recognised complication of diphtheria toxin; diphtheria's cardiac complication is myocarditis from direct toxin injury to the myocardium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pericarditis is not the classic diphtheria cardiac complication; the toxin's target is the myocardium itself, producing myocarditis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vasculitis is not a recognised complication of diphtheria toxin; the toxin's recognised target organs are the myocardium and peripheral nerves.

questions.learning_objective: State that myocarditis is a recognised toxin-mediated complication of Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q6, key p.9.
questions.title: Most common cause of pericarditis
questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of Pericarditis?

explanations.A: Correct. Among bacterial and mycobacterial causes, Staphylococcus aureus (typically producing purulent pericarditis by haematogenous spread) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (producing tuberculous pericarditis, especially where tuberculosis is endemic) are cited as the most common causes of pericarditis overall. Because these two organisms account for the largest share of infective pericarditis, they anchor empirical antimicrobial choices and the differential diagnosis when a bacterial or mycobacterial cause of pericarditis is suspected.
explanations.B: Incorrect. While both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae can cause purulent pericarditis, this pairing omits M. tuberculosis, which is cited alongside S. aureus as the most common overall cause.
explanations.C: Incorrect. S. pneumoniae and Coxsackievirus are each recognised causes of pericarditis, but this pairing is not the combination cited as the most common overall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Histoplasma capsulatum and Echovirus are recognised but less common causes of pericarditis, not the most common pairing.

questions.learning_objective: State that Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are cited as the most common causes of pericarditis.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q7, key p.9.
questions.title: Treatment for endocarditis
questions.question: Which of the following is the treatment for endocarditis?

explanations.A: Correct. Standard antimicrobial treatment for infective endocarditis combines a cell-wall-active agent such as penicillin (or vancomycin) with an aminoglycoside. Penicillin weakens the bacterial cell wall, which lets the aminoglycoside -- normally excluded by an intact cell wall -- enter the cell and act on the ribosome, producing synergistic, more rapid bactericidal killing than either drug achieves alone. This synergy is important because the vegetation in endocarditis is a dense, poorly vascularised mass that is harder for antibiotics and host defences to penetrate than an ordinary soft-tissue infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Penicillin alone lacks the synergistic bactericidal speed of the combination and is not the standard approach for a poorly vascularised vegetation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ceftriaxone alone is used in specific circumstances but is not the general standard combination described in this teaching.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A recognised standard combination (penicillin/vancomycin plus an aminoglycoside) does exist, so 'none of the above' is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that infective endocarditis treatment combines penicillin (or vancomycin) with an aminoglycoside for synergistic bactericidal effect.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q7, key p.9.
questions.title: Feature of Coxsackie B virus infection in infants
questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of Coxsackie B virus infection in infants?

options.B: Generalized disease affecting heart, liver, and brain

explanations.A: Incorrect. Herpangina, a vesicular throat illness, is more characteristic of Coxsackievirus A infection in older children, not the severe pattern seen in infants with group B.
explanations.B: Correct. In neonates and young infants, Coxsackievirus B infection can cause a severe, generalised disease with multi-organ involvement -- myocarditis, hepatitis and meningoencephalitis together -- rather than the milder, more localised illness typical in older children and adults. Without the protective effect of a fully developed immune system, the virus can disseminate widely in an infant, simultaneously affecting the heart, liver and brain. This generalised, multi-organ pattern makes neonatal Coxsackievirus B infection a much higher-mortality disease than the disease in older patients.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is a Coxsackievirus A (and enterovirus 71) illness, not the generalised group-B pattern seen in infants.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis is associated with enterovirus 70 and Coxsackievirus A24, not the generalised infant disease pattern of group B.

questions.learning_objective: State that Coxsackievirus B causes a severe generalised disease affecting heart, liver and brain in infants.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q8, key p.9.
questions.title: Common cause of myocarditis in immunocompromised patients
questions.question: Which of the following organisms is a common cause of myocarditis in immunocompromised patients?

explanations.A: Correct. In immunocompromised patients, Candida albicans is a recognised opportunistic cause of myocarditis. It can invade the bloodstream (candidaemia) and disseminate haematogenously to seed the myocardium, producing fungal myocarditis that a competent immune system would normally prevent. Recognising Candida as a cause of myocarditis specifically in immunocompromised patients -- unlike the largely viral aetiology of myocarditis in healthy hosts -- should prompt consideration of antifungal therapy when this population presents with new cardiac dysfunction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Streptococcus pyogenes causes rheumatic carditis by an immune mechanism, not opportunistic myocarditis specific to immunocompromised patients.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) can cause carditis, but it is not the organism specifically associated with opportunistic myocarditis in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a rare cause of myocarditis in the general population, not the classic opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised patients.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Candida albicans as a recognised opportunistic cause of myocarditis in immunocompromised patients.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q8, key p.9.
questions.title: Symptom that is NOT typical of acute infective endocarditis
questions.question: Which of the following is not a typical symptom of acute endocarditis?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS typical). High fever is a classic feature of acute infective endocarditis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS typical). A new regurgitant heart murmur is a classic feature of acute infective endocarditis.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS typical). Painless macular lesions on the palms/soles (Janeway lesions) are a classic embolic feature of acute infective endocarditis.
explanations.D: Correct. Migratory polyarthritis -- large-joint arthritis that moves from joint to joint -- is not a typical symptom of acute infective endocarditis. Acute endocarditis is a direct bacterial infection of the heart valve producing fever, a new murmur and embolic phenomena from septic emboli; it is not an immune-mediated process affecting the joints the way rheumatic fever is. Migratory polyarthritis is instead a major feature of the distinct, immune-mediated disease rheumatic fever, and distinguishing the two syndromes by this feature is a common exam discriminator.

questions.learning_objective: State that migratory polyarthritis is not typical of acute infective endocarditis; it is instead a feature of rheumatic fever.
